open-question.question: Does an install or update of the Gurita plugin started from the Settings window run in a terminal the person can watch, as a recipe run does, or as a background process like the harness check, with the window reporting how it ended?
open-question.alternative: An install or update runs in a terminal the extension opens and shows, as a recipe run does: the terminal's own process runs the harness's install or update commands in the runner's session shell at the project root, its output and any prompt visible and answerable there. The window learns only that the terminal was started and, at most, that it closed; it reports no outcome of its own, and the person reads how it ended in the terminal. It reuses the one way the extension already starts long, visible work (`src/runs.ts` launching a terminal), so every line the CLIs print and any prompt they raise reach the person directly, which matters while no install or update command has yet been run against a harness and what each prints or asks is unobserved. The window has no outcome to show beside the harness, so a failed install looks the same in the Settings window as a successful one until the person reads the terminal or uses Check again; and it leaves a terminal per install for the person to read and close.

An install or update runs in a terminal the extension opens and shows, as in a recipe run, its output and any prompt visible and answerable there, and the extension also watches that terminal's process end (its exit status, through the terminal or a VS Code task run in the terminal panel) and the window then reports how it ended, success or failure, beside the harness or in a notification. It gives the person both the full live output, with prompts answerable, and an outcome the window states without anyone reading the terminal, so an unexpected prompt or long download stays visible while the window still knows whether the install succeeded. The run terminals today report only that they closed, never an exit status, so the extension gains a second terminal mechanism with exit-status tracking; the window can tell success from failure only by the exit code, so a command that exits 0 after printing a warning reads as a success, and the reported reason for a failure is whatever the person reads in the terminal.

An install or update runs as a child process with no terminal, as the harness check does: started through `execFile` into the runner's session shell (`$SHELL -i` for the sh, bash, zsh family) at the project root with a time limit, its input closed and the commands given their non-interactive flags (such as `-y`), its output captured and not shown. While it runs the window shows the harness as busy and disables its controls, and when it ends the window reports success or failure, the failure with the captured error text, in the harness's line or an error notification as other edits' failures are told. It keeps the whole action inside the Settings window, mirrors the harness check's tested pattern (session shell, captured print, a stated result), and gives the window the exit status and the error text to report, with no terminal for the person to manage. Nothing the commands print is visible while they run, so a slow download looks stalled and a command that waits on a prompt hangs until the time limit; whether the CLIs prompt or run long is unobserved, the condition the hands-on command verification question settles.

An install or update runs as a background child process in the runner's session shell, as the harness check does, its input closed and the commands given their non-interactive flags, but its output is streamed line by line into a VS Code output channel of the extension's, which the person can open while it runs and which is brought forward when the run fails. The window shows the harness as busy while it runs and, when it ends, reports success or failure beside the harness or in a notification. The window owns the outcome as in a plain background run, while every line the commands print stays available on demand and surfaces by itself on a failure, so a stall or an unexpected message can be diagnosed without a terminal per install. It adds an output channel, a mechanism the extension does not use today, and streaming instead of the check's captured print; like any background run it cannot answer a prompt, so a command that asks for input hangs until the time limit, the condition the hands-on command verification question settles.

open-question.question: Which ref of a harness's distribution repository (`uHappyLogic/gurita-<host>`) is the latest published release that an install or update fetches: the tip of `main`, which the documented installs fetch, or the highest version tag or the latest GitHub release?

Installing the latest published release can leave a copy whose version differs from the one the extension was packaged from, which the harness check today reports as a failed check. Once the Settings window can install and update, which version is an installed copy compared with: the packaged version as today, the latest published version read from the distribution repository, or both? And if the latest published version is read, is it read with every harness check or only when the person asks?
open-question.alternative: The installed copy is compared with the packaged version (`bundled/plugin_version.txt`) alone, by the exact string equality `src/harnessCheck.ts` uses now, a differing version, newer or older, still counting as the failed `version` check. The latest published version is never read, so the check stays offline and unchanged. Nothing in the check, its script, its tests, or its README section changes, the extension still contacts no network on a check, and it keeps the stance the overlapping marketplace-publication mission states, that the check comparing with the packaged version stays as it is. An install or update from the window that fetches a release newer than the package leaves the harness reported as failed immediately after a successful install, so the window's own action produces the failure the question describes, and the window can never tell the person whether a newer release exists.

The installed copy is compared with the packaged version alone, but as a minimum rather than an equality: a copy older than the packaged version fails the `version` check, a copy equal to or newer than it passes. The latest published version is never read, and the check stays offline. A copy brought up to the latest release by the window no longer shows as failed, while an outdated copy that may lack what the packaged extension expects still does, all without any network read or new latency in the check. The check needs a version ordering it does not have today (it compares strings only), and it still cannot tell the person whether a newer release is published, so an up-to-date-looking copy may be behind the distribution repository; it also departs from the marketplace-publication mission's stated premise that the check stays as it is.

The installed copy's version is shown without being compared with anything: neither the packaged version nor the latest published version counts toward the check, which fails only on a missing CLI or a missing or disabled plugin. Nothing reads a distribution repository. The simplest check that can never report a window-made install as failed, staying offline and dropping the version branch rather than adding ordering or network code. The check loses every version signal: an old copy that no longer matches what the extension's recipes expect passes silently, and nothing tells the person an update is available, leaving Update a blind control.

The packaged version no longer enters the comparison; the installed copy is compared with the latest published version read from the harness's distribution repository, and that read runs as part of every harness check, the first opening of the window in a session and every Check again alike. The comparison matches exactly what Install and Update fetch, so a freshly installed copy reads as current and an outdated one is reported each time the window shows the check, with no extra control to learn. Every check now contacts the network for each harness, adding latency inside the 120-second limit and a new failure mode offline or under rate limits that must not read as a failed install, and the compatibility signal between the extension and the plugin is lost; what counts as latest depends on the ref the published-release question settles.

The packaged version no longer enters the comparison, and the ordinary harness check reports the installed version without a version verdict; the latest published version is read only when the person asks, through a control of its own in the Settings window, and the installed copy is compared with it then. The routine check stays offline and as fast as today, and the network is contacted only on an explicit request, while the comparison the person does ask for is with the release Update would actually fetch. Until the person asks, nothing flags an outdated or incompatible copy, the window gains one more control and a second, separately kept result, and whether Update is offered before any request is made depends on how the update-availability question settles.

The installed copy is compared with both versions on every harness check: with the packaged version as a floor, a copy older than it failing the check, and with the latest published version read from the distribution repository, a copy older than that shown as having an update available rather than as a failure. The two comparisons answer two different things, compatibility with this extension and currency against the published release, so a window-made install of a newer release passes while both an incompatible copy and an outdated one are told apart on every view. It carries both costs at once: a version ordering the check lacks today and a network read for every harness on every check, with offline and rate-limit outcomes to tell apart from install failures, plus a second verdict per harness for the page to draw and the tests to cover.

The ordinary harness check compares the installed copy with the packaged version as a floor, offline, a copy older than it failing; the latest published version is read only when the person asks, through a control of its own, and a copy older than it is then shown as having an update available. The routine check keeps its offline speed and gains a compatibility verdict that a window-made install no longer trips, while the published-release comparison is there on demand without making every check depend on the network. It is the largest change to the window and the check: version ordering, a new control, and a second result kept beside the session-kept check, and an outdated but compatible copy goes unflagged until the person asks; how the update control behaves before that request depends on the update-availability question.

open-question.question: For a harness that has a Gurita copy installed, is the Update control in the Settings window offered always, or only when the installed copy's version is found to differ from the version it is compared with?
open-question.alternative: Update is offered for every harness whose check found the CLI and an installed Gurita copy. The version comparison does not gate it: a copy whose version matches the compared version gets the same enabled Update control as one that differs, and the check line beside it still reports whether the versions differ. Whatever the comparison baseline turns out to be, the person can always bring a copy to the latest published release. A matching packaged version does not mean the copy is the latest published one, a version that could not be read does not hide the control, and running Update over a matching copy re-fetches the release, which also repairs a damaged copy (on Antigravity, re-extracting the archive). The window also needs no version rule of its own and no state for the control to go stale against. The control does not tell the person whether updating will change anything, so they may run an install that is a no-op (Claude Code's `claude plugin update` on a current copy, for example) or start one they did not need. Whether that clutter or wasted run matters depends on how an update runs and whether it asks for confirmation, both axes sibling questions own.

Update is offered only when the installed copy's version differs from the version it is compared with, in either direction. It is not offered when the two are equal. When the comparison cannot be made, because the installed version or the compared version could not be read, Update is offered. The control appears exactly when the check already reports a version difference, so the two agree and an equal copy gets no pointless update. Failing open means an unreadable version or a failed read of the compared version never leaves the person with no way to update. A copy whose version equals the compared version can never be updated or repaired from the window. If the comparison is with the packaged version, a copy equal to the packaged version gets no Update even when a newer release has been published. That depends on the comparison baseline, an axis a sibling question owns. Treating any difference as a reason to update also offers an update to a copy newer than the compared version, which could move it to an older release when the compared version is the latest published one.

Update is offered only when the installed copy's version differs from the version it is compared with, in either direction. It is not offered when the two are equal, and it is not offered when the comparison cannot be made because either version could not be read. Update is offered only when the window has positive evidence that the copy is out of line, so a click on it always has a known version difference behind it and the control never invites an update the window cannot justify. A failed or not-yet-made read blocks updates: a listing error, a version the check could not read, or a compared version read only when asked for or not reachable over the network leaves no update path in the window. How often that happens depends on the comparison baseline and when it is read, axes a sibling question owns. The equal-version and newer-copy costs of the previous option apply here too.

Update is offered only when the installed copy's version is older than the version it is compared with, read as a MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH ordering. It is not offered when the copy is equal or newer. When the comparison cannot be made, because a version could not be read or does not parse as MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, Update is offered. The window never invites an update that would move a copy backwards, for example a copy ahead of the published release or newer than the packaged version, while an unreadable version still leaves an update path. The window needs a version ordering of its own, beyond the equality the check compares today, and a copy that is equal or newer can never be updated or repaired from the window. As with any gated option, a copy equal to the packaged version gets no Update when a newer release exists if the comparison is with the packaged version. That depends on the comparison baseline, an axis a sibling question owns.

Update is offered only when the installed copy's version is older than the version it is compared with, read as a MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH ordering. It is not offered when the copy is equal or newer, and it is not offered when the comparison cannot be made because a version could not be read or does not parse. This is the strictest gate: Update appears only when the window knows the copy is behind, so every update it offers moves the copy forward and none is speculative. It combines the costs of the other gates: the window needs a version ordering of its own, equal and newer copies can never be updated or repaired, and any failed or not-yet-made version read leaves no update path. How often that read is missing depends on the comparison baseline and when it is read, axes a sibling question owns.

open-question.question: A harness's existing Gurita copy, or its marketplace named `gurita`, may come from somewhere other than the distribution repository, for example a local checkout registered as a directory marketplace under the same name and plugin id. What does Install or Update in the Settings window do on such a harness: switch it to the distribution repository, update from the source already registered, or refuse and say why?

No install, update, or marketplace command has yet been run against any harness, so what each prints, whether it prompts, and how long it takes are unknown, and the copies on the maintainer's machine are installed from the local checkout. How does the mission observe the commands before building on them: by running them against those real installations, by running them against a separate configuration home per harness, or not at all, relying on each CLI's help text?
How does the person pick the scope of a Claude Code install (user, project, or local) in the Settings window, whose page holds buttons and dropdowns only?
open-question.alternative: The Claude Code row of the Harnesses part carries a scope dropdown (a `select` of user, project, and local) beside its Install control, the form the page already uses for its model, effort, and harness dropdowns; the selection lives in the page's state for the window's session only, is stored nowhere, starts at user (the CLI's own default for `claude plugin install -s`), and a click on Install installs at the scope the dropdown shows. The scope is visible before the click and uses a control the page already draws and tests, so the person sees exactly what Install will do with no extra dialog step and nothing new is persisted. The row gains a control that only Claude Code has, and a person who clicks Install without looking installs at user scope by default; which scopes the dropdown lists while a copy already stands, or while no folder is open, depends on the sibling questions on installing beside an existing copy and on project scopes without a project.

The Claude Code row carries a scope dropdown (user, project, local) whose value is a stored setting in the per-user `~/.gurita/variants.json`, where everything else the settings hold is kept, read back on every opening of the window and used by every Install until the person changes it; the first value is user. A person who always installs at one scope sets it once and every later install from any window or session follows it, consistent with the rule that the settings' values are kept in `variants.json`. A per-user stored value is applied to every project, so a project or local choice made for one repository silently carries into the next, where it writes that project's `.claude/settings.json` or local settings unasked; it adds a stored field and its read and write path to the settings file for a choice that is usually made once per install, and whether Update also follows it depends on the sibling question on update target scopes.

The Claude Code row carries no dropdown and instead three install controls, Install at user, Install at project, and Install at local, each installing at its own scope on a click, with nothing selected or stored. The scope is part of the control the person clicks, so there is no default to fall into and no hidden state, and each control can be enabled or disabled on its own as the scope's situation requires. Three buttons crowd one row where the other harnesses show a single Install, and the row grows further if update controls follow the same per-scope pattern; which of the three are shown or enabled depends on the sibling questions on installing beside an existing copy and on project scopes without a project.

The Claude Code row carries one Install control like the other harnesses; clicking it opens VS Code's own quick pick (`showQuickPick`, which the extension already uses to pick a starting variant) listing user, project, and local, each with a one-line description of where it is recorded (user settings, the project's shared `.claude/settings.json`, the project's local settings), and the install runs at the scope picked, a dismissed pick installing nothing; nothing is selected or stored on the page. The page keeps one Install control per harness and the choice is made at the moment of installing with room to explain each scope, so a project-scope write to a tracked file is never made without the person reading what it means. Every Claude Code install costs a second step and moves the choice out of the page into a picker the page tests cannot draw, so the stubbed `showQuickPick` becomes the only test of it; whether the picker also serves as the confirmation before installing depends on the sibling question on confirmation before install.

open-question.question: When Claude Code already holds a Gurita copy at one scope, does the Settings window still offer installing at the other scopes, or is Install offered only while no copy applies to the open project?
open-question.alternative: While Claude Code holds a Gurita copy at one or more scopes that apply to the open project, the Settings window still offers Install for Claude Code, at every one of the three scopes (user, project, local) that holds no copy applying to the project, whether that scope is more or less specific than the copy that wins; a scope already holding an applying copy is not offered for Install, that copy being reached through Update. Copies at project or local scope recorded for other project roots do not count, since they do not apply to the open project. It offers exactly the scopes Claude Code itself supports and leaves the person free to add any of them, such as a project-scope copy pinned in the tracked `.claude/settings.json` for teammates beside a personal user-scope copy (the arrangement this machine already holds), so the window never withholds a native install path. It lets the window create several copies at once, so a person can install a more specific copy that silently shadows the one in use, or a less specific one that changes nothing for the open project, and every multi-copy question (which copy Update acts on, how several scopes are shown) becomes reachable from the window itself; the window also needs per-scope detection, which today's check, reporting one copy and no scope, does not give.

While a copy applies to the open project, Install is offered only at the scopes more specific than the copy that wins for the project, in Claude Code's own order (local over project over user): with a user-scope winner, project and local are offered; with a project-scope winner, local alone; with a local-scope winner, no Install is offered. Less specific scopes are not offered while a copy applies. Every install the window offers is one that takes effect in the open project, replacing the copy that wins there, so no click produces a copy the person cannot see working from where they clicked it. A person holding only a project or local copy cannot add a user-scope copy for all their projects from this project's window and must open a project with no applying copy or use the CLI, and each offered install shadows the existing copy, which may then sit unused at its own version; it too needs the winning copy's scope, which today's check does not report.

While a copy applies to the open project, Install is offered only at the scopes less specific than the copy that wins for the project: with a local-scope winner, project and user are offered; with a project-scope winner, user alone; with a user-scope winner, no Install is offered. More specific scopes are not offered while a copy applies. No install from the window changes which copy the open project runs, so adding a copy beside an existing one can never displace the copy the person's runs already use; it still covers the common case of widening a project-only copy to the user scope. The copy it installs never shows its effect in the open project, so the window would report an install the person cannot observe from here, and pinning a project or local copy over an existing user copy (a team's tracked `.claude/settings.json` entry) is never offered beside a user-scope copy.

alternative.id: No Install once a copy applies

open-question.alternative: Install for Claude Code is offered only while no Gurita copy applies to the open project; as soon as one does, at any scope, Install is not offered at any scope and the existing copy is reached only through Update. Adding a copy at another scope beside it is left to the CLI. It is the simplest model: one control per state (Install when absent, Update when present), the window never creates a second copy, and it needs only the check's existing installed-or-not answer to decide, not per-scope detection. It withholds scopes the goal says Claude Code offers natively, so a person with a user-scope copy who wants a project-scope copy for the repository must leave the window for the CLI; how a copy counts as applying when the winning entry is disabled is a condition owned by the disabled-copy question.

open-question.question: When Claude Code holds Gurita copies at more than one scope that applies to the open project, which does Update in the Settings window act on: every detected scope, only the copy that wins for the project, or one scope the person picks?

For a Claude Code install at project or local scope made from the Settings window, at which scope is the `gurita` marketplace registered: the user scope, where `claude plugin install --marketplace` adds a marketplace not yet known, or the same scope as the install, through `claude plugin marketplace add --scope`?

When Claude Code holds Gurita copies at several scopes that apply to the open project, does the Settings window show the scope names alone beside the version of the one copy that wins for the project, or each scope with its own version?

When the Claude Code entry that wins for the open project is disabled, the harness check counts Gurita as not installed. How does the Settings window treat such a copy: is its scope shown as a detected scope, and is Install offered for a scope that already holds a disabled copy?

Claude Code's project and local scopes belong to a project root. What does the Settings window offer for those two scopes when no workspace folder is open, so that the root it works from is the home directory?

An install or update changes a harness's configuration, and at Claude Code's project scope the project's own `.claude/settings.json`. Does a click on Install or Update in the Settings window start it at once, or does the window ask for a confirmation first?

Antigravity's documented install is a `curl` and `tar` pipeline that extracts the distribution repository's archive into `~/.gemini/config/plugins/gurita`, while `agy plugin install <target>` exists but has only been seen to accept a directory. Which does the Settings window's Antigravity install use?

Antigravity has no update command. When an update from the Settings window brings a newer release into the existing plugin directory `~/.gemini/config/plugins/gurita`, are the new files laid over the old ones, which keeps files the new release no longer ships, or is the directory's content replaced whole?

The harness check's result is kept for the extension's session and only Check again runs it afresh. After an install or update ends, does the Settings window run the check again by itself, or keep showing the earlier result until Check again is used?

Claude Code says an updated plugin needs a restart to apply, and Antigravity discovers a new plugin directory only when a session starts. After an install or update, does the Settings window tell the person that running harness sessions must be restarted?
